summary: In Hebrew the words that point to or stand for a noun copy its gender and number: the demonstratives (זֶה / זֹאת / אֵלֶּה; הַהוּא / הַהִיא / הָהֵם / הָהֵן), the pronoun that replaces it (הַכּוֹס? הִיא שָׁם — כּוֹס is feminine), and the verb “to be” in the past and future (הַשֻּׁלְחָן הָיָה פֹּה, הַמִּטָּה הָיְתָה שָׁם, הַסְּפָרִים הָיוּ פֹּה). A demonstrative after a noun also copies its definiteness: הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה, both with the article. Adjectives (lesson 16) and present-tense verbs (lesson 7) will agree in the same way. What counts is the noun’s grammatical gender, not its ending: הַחַלּוֹנוֹת הָהֵם (m.), הַנָּשִׁים הָהֵן (f.). A mixed group is masculine.

blocks.caption: How to make a word agree

blocks.title: The ending can lie
blocks.text: חַלּוֹנוֹת, קִירוֹת, כִּסְּאוֹת, מַפְתְּחוֹת are masculine: הַכִּסְּאוֹת? הֵם שָׁם. נָשִׁים is feminine: הַנָּשִׁים הָהֵן.

blocks.title: Definiteness agrees too
blocks.text: After a definite noun, the demonstrative takes הַ as well: הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה, הַדִּירָה הַהִיא. This is the same rule that will make adjectives take הַ: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל “the big house” (lesson 16).

items.title: Hebrew
points: agreement in gender and number (+ definiteness after the noun)
הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה — plural agreement for things too

items.title: German
points: agreement in gender, number and case
dieser Tisch / diese Lampe / dieses Bett

items.title: Arabic
points: plural things take feminine singular: هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ “these books”

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Which noun does this word belong to?
Is that noun masculine or feminine (look at the singular)?

askYourself: Which noun does the word refer to?
What is that noun’s gender — from the singular and the exception list, not from the plural ending?
Is it singular or plural? Is it a mixed group (→ masculine)?
Is the noun definite? Then a demonstrative after it takes הַ too.
Which word must agree: a demonstrative, a pronoun, or a form of הָיָה?
steps: Pick the matching demonstrative / pronoun / form of הָיָה.
Add הַ if the noun is definite.

traps: *הַחַלּוֹנוֹת הָהֵן — חַלּוֹן is masculine: הַחַלּוֹנוֹת הָהֵם.
*הַכּוֹס? הוּא שָׁם — כּוֹס is feminine: הִיא שָׁם.
*הַמִּטָּה הָיָה שָׁם — the past agrees: הַמִּטָּה הָיְתָה שָׁם.
*הַסֵּפֶר זֶה — after a definite noun use הַזֶּה.
Unlike Arabic, plural things take plural agreement: הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, הֵם.

seeAlso.note: Arabic agrees in gender, number, case and definiteness — and gives non-human plurals feminine singular agreement (هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ), which Hebrew never does.
German articles, demonstratives and adjectives agree in gender, number and case (dieser Tisch, diese Lampe, dieses Bett).
Chinese has no agreement: 这 and the verb never change for the noun.

notes.text: Greek agreement also covers gender and number (αυτό το βιβλίο, αυτή η λάμπα) — and case, which Hebrew lacks; Hebrew instead copies definiteness: הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה.
As in Russian, the words copy gender and number, and the past of “to be” agrees (был / была / были ~ הָיָה / הָיְתָה / הָיוּ). Hebrew has no case to copy, but copies the article instead.
As in Spanish, gender and number agree (esta lámpara, estos libros ~ הַמְּנוֹרָה הַזֹּאת, הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה); new is that the article is copied too.
English agreement is little more than this / these; in Hebrew pronouns, demonstratives, adjectives and verbs copy the noun’s gender and number, and a word after a definite noun takes the article too.
Like ce / cette / ces and il / elle, Hebrew words copy gender and number; in addition a demonstrative or adjective after a definite noun takes the article: הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה.
German agreement adds case (diesen Tisch, diesem Tisch); Hebrew has no cases but copies definiteness: הַשֻּׁלְחָן הַזֶּה.
Hindi verbs and many adjectives copy gender and number (अच्छा लड़का / अच्छी लड़की); Hebrew does the same with demonstratives, pronouns, adjectives and verbs.
Persian has no gender agreement; in Hebrew pronouns, demonstratives, adjectives and verbs copy the noun’s gender and number.
Marathi words copy gender and number (हा मुलगा / ही मुलगी), much as Hebrew does (הַיֶּלֶד הַזֶּה / הַיַּלְדָּה הַזֹּאת); Hebrew has no neuter.
In Arabic a plural of things takes feminine singular agreement (هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ); Hebrew never does: הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, הֵם פֹּה.
Turkish has no gender agreement; Hebrew makes every word that points to a noun copy its gender and number.
Japanese words do not agree with nouns; in Hebrew demonstratives, pronouns and verbs change with the noun’s gender and number.
Finnish agreement copies number and case (tässä talossa); Hebrew copies gender, number and definiteness — never case.
Hungarian adjectives and demonstratives before a noun copy no gender; Hebrew words after a noun copy its gender, number and definiteness.
Agreement is at the heart of Swahili (kitabu hiki, vitabu hivi); Hebrew works the same way with two genders instead of many classes.
As with Luganda class agreement (ekitabo kino, ebitabo bino), every Hebrew word that points to a noun copies it — with two genders and the plural, marked by endings.
Chinese words never change for agreement; in Hebrew demonstratives, pronouns, adjectives and verbs change for the noun’s gender and number.
Vietnamese words never change for agreement; Hebrew words that point to a noun copy its gender and number.
Inuktitut words agree in number (singular, dual, plural) and case, not in gender; Hebrew agreement is gender and number, plus the article.
